zone: The Gardner group above the Methow
_areas_note: Two peaks survive verification here and they are the pair the file is named for: Gardner Mountain and North Gardner Mountain, a mile apart on the same ridge above the head of Wolf Creek, with North Gardner the county highpoint and the higher of the two. Two ways in serve them and both are described. The Cedar Creek trailhead, off the North Cascades Highway about four miles from Mazama and half a mile past Klipchuck Campground, puts a party on the west side of the group by way of the Cedar Creek trail past Cedar Falls and up toward Abernathy Pass — this is the shorter approach and the one to take when there is still spring snow, since the trail is low and opens early. The Wolf Creek trail from near Winthrop is the standard summer approach: about ten miles up the valley bottom to Gardner Meadows directly beneath the peaks, and it is the way almost everyone climbs them. Both are Methow Valley district trails and both stage out of the same small town, so they are one zone. TWO PEAKS WERE REMOVED. Mount Bigelow is not served by either trailhead in this file. It is the fifth-highest summit on Sawtooth Ridge and the southernmost point of the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, and its summit stands about 1,300 ft above Upper Eagle Lake in barely a third of a mile — the standard approach is the Eagle Lake trail from the Crater Creek trailhead on the Gold Creek road out of the lower Methow, roughly 45 road miles from the Twisp River. Its north side does drain to East Fork Buttermilk Creek, which is presumably where the Twisp River grouping came from, but no one climbs it that way and the camp it actually uses, Upper Eagle Lake at Horsehead Pass, is already recorded in the Sawtooth Ridge and Lake Chelan shore zone. Chelan Butte is not an alpine objective in any sense. It is a 3,835 ft sagebrush and grass butte standing between the foot of Lake Chelan and the Columbia, on a state wildlife area above the town of Chelan, with a dirt road running the whole way to the old lookout site on the summit and a well-known hang gliding and paragliding launch on top. People hike the road for the view and the spring flowers, and it is a fine walk, but there is no climbing on it, no backcountry camping worth recording, and nothing that any trailhead in this file reaches. It has been left out of areas entirely rather than given manufactured camping. Nothing recorded for the Sawtooth Ridge and Lake Chelan shore zone is repeated here: Scatter Lake, the Reynolds Creek basin, the Oval Lakes, Libby Lake, Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass, Boiling Lake, Prince Creek and Bird Creek are all covered there and none of them appears below. On current conditions — the North Cascades Highway opened unusually late in 2026 after repair work and there is a paving programme closing several trailheads and sites along the highway corridor between early August and mid September, concentrated at and near Washington Pass. The Methow district's active fire closure this season is in the Pasayten, north of the highway, and does not reach Cedar Creek or Wolf Creek. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have banned campfires on all Okanogan-Wenatchee land since early July, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban on top of that.

sites.name: Klipchuck Campground and the Highway 20 road-head campgrounds
sites.capacity: Around forty sites at Klipchuck; the smaller campgrounds up and down the highway corridor add a few dozen more between them
sites.water: Piped water at Klipchuck when the season's system is turned on, and Early Winters Creek nearby. Do not count on the tap outside the main season or in a drought year — check before you drive out, because the alternative is hauling water from town.
sites.permit: Nightly campground fee. Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for the trailhead lots. No wilderness permit required. Campfires are prohibited under the forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions currently in force, including in established rings, and the county burn ban applies as well. Some highway-corridor sites are closed in rotation for paving work between early August and mid September.
sites.notes: The obvious place to sleep before starting up either side of the Gardners, and the only one in this file with running water and a toilet. It sits in ponderosa forest just off the highway about four miles beyond Mazama, and the Cedar Creek trailhead is roughly half a mile further along a short forest road — near enough to walk to if you wanted. Coming from the west over the pass, this is the first campground on the dry side and the change is abrupt: open pine, no undergrowth, hot afternoons and cold clear nights. Use it as staging, not as a destination. The practical value is that it lets you drive out the evening before, sleep at the trailhead, and start the long Wolf Creek or Cedar Creek walk at dawn rather than in the heat of the day, which on these approaches matters more than it sounds. Bear in mind the highway itself opened late in 2026 after repair work, and paving through this corridor has been closing individual sites for stretches of a week or so at a time; ring ahead rather than arriving on spec.

sites.name: Gardner Meadows, Wolf Creek trail
sites.capacity: Numerous comfortable sites through the meadows and in the trees at their edge; this is the one place in the zone that will absorb several parties without crowding
sites.water: A small stream flows south out of Gardner Mountain through the meadows and there is water at camp through a normal summer. This is the critical fill point: the Wolf Creek trail below is notably short of water for a valley-bottom trail, and everything above the meadows is bone dry. Carry the whole day's supply for the climb, and in a heat wave carry water up the approach as well — parties have turned around on these peaks for want of it.
sites.permit: The upper Wolf Creek trail enters the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No wilderness permit or quota to hike or camp; sign the trailhead register. Party size limited to twelve people and eighteen head of stock. Northwest Forest Pass at the Wolf Creek trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide restrictions, and in a burned valley with standing snags this is a rule worth taking seriously. Proper food storage required.
sites.notes: This is the basecamp for both peaks and the way the great majority of parties climb them. The Wolf Creek trail runs roughly ten miles up the valley bottom from the trailhead near Winthrop to meadows sitting directly beneath Gardner Mountain, with North Gardner a mile further northwest along the connecting ridge. From here a fit party can take both summits in a single long day and walk out the next morning. Know what the approach is now: the first eight miles or so run through forest burned in the 2021 fire, so there is very little shade, the tread is crossed by blowdown in places, and the second half is brushy. Where the trail turns uphill into the meadows it becomes genuinely hard to follow, buried in downed logs and regrowth, and one of the creek crossings is easy to miss even in daylight — this is not a route to be finding for the first time in the dark. Allow four and a half to five hours to camp with a climbing load. Season is July through September; the aspect is dry and eastern so the snow leaves early, but the same thing that clears the snow makes the walk in punishing in midsummer heat. The climbing above is a scramble on loose scree with pinnacles and short cliff bands on the connecting ridge that force you off the crest rather than along it.

sites.name: High basin camp above Gardner Meadows
sites.capacity: A small soggy basin with room for one or two tents; a party of two or three at most
sites.water: A seep and small stream in the basin, which is what makes the site usable at all — it is boggy underfoot in early season and can be dry by late August in a poor snow year. Confirm it before carrying up on the strength of it, because there is no second option at this elevation and the retreat is all the way back to the meadows.
sites.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No permit or quota, party limit of twelve, food stored properly. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions apply and there is nothing worth burning up here in any case. Camp on durable ground and off the wet meadow.
sites.notes: The higher option for a party that wants to shorten summit day rather than take both peaks in one long push from the meadows. Heading north out of Gardner Meadows the ground rises to a small meadow basin at about 6,200 ft, and an old boot path leaves the main trail a few hundred feet west of the small stream to reach it. Stay between roughly 6,200 and 6,400 ft on the way across — drop lower and you land in groves of silver snags with jack-strawed deadfall that cost far more time than the elevation saves. From a camp here the scree slope to the ridge is about 1,400 ft of gain in half a mile, which is the steepest and loosest section of the whole climb and much better done early and on firm ground. It is an exposed spot with no shelter to speak of and it is cold; the compensation is the position and the head start. Use it when the forecast is settled and when you have confirmed water. In a dry August the meadows below are the safer plan.

sites.name: Cedar Creek meadow camps above the falls
sites.capacity: Good established sites for hikers and stock where the trail enters the meadows; several parties can spread out
sites.water: Cedar Creek runs alongside for the whole approach and through the meadows, and it is the most dependable water in this file — a snow-fed creek in a north-facing valley that holds well into autumn. Fill here, because the climb east out of the valley toward the Gardner ridge has nothing.
sites.permit: The Cedar Creek trail is outside the wilderness until it nears Abernathy Pass, where it enters the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No permit or quota either side of that line; party limit of twelve inside. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Campfires prohibited under the forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions and the county burn ban.
sites.notes: The western approach camp, and the reason to use this side at all. Cedar Falls comes at about 1.7 miles from the trailhead and is the day-hike turnaround for most visitors; keep going and roughly two miles beyond the falls the trail opens into meadows with good camping. From here the head of the valley and the west flank of North Gardner are within reach, and this is materially shorter than coming round by Wolf Creek. Its real value is seasonal. The trailhead is low and this is one of the first trails in the area to melt out, so in a late spring when Wolf Creek is still buried and the Gardner Meadows approach is a slog, this side goes. The trade is snow higher up and a steeper, less travelled finish. Damage from the 2021 fire is visible in this drainage too, heavier away from the creek than beside it, and the lower trail to the falls is in good order. The trail continues to Abernathy Pass at about 9.2 miles and over into North Creek, which is a useful escape or through-route if weather closes the tops.

sites.name: Upper Cedar Creek head basin
sites.capacity: Informal ground for one or two small parties; no established sites and no flat obvious platform
sites.water: Snowmelt and the headwaters of Cedar Creek. Reliable in early season, which is when this camp makes sense; in late summer it thins out and the meadows below the falls become the better choice. Melting snow is the normal answer here in spring.
sites.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness at the head of the valley. No permit, no quota, party limit of twelve, proper food storage. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions, and there is no fuel. Leave no trace on unestablished ground and camp on rock or snow rather than fragile meadow.
sites.notes: A spring and early-summer bivouac rather than a camp, used by parties taking the west side of North Gardner when snow still covers the ground. Getting into the head of the valley involves leaving the maintained trail and working up through brush, and it is not pleasant in dry conditions — the argument for it is precisely that on snow the brush is buried and the travel is fast. From the basin the west and southwest flanks of North Gardner rise directly, and a party can take both Gardner summits and be back at the car the following morning, which is appreciably shorter than the Wolf Creek round trip. Expect avalanche terrain on those slopes into June and treat the timing accordingly: an early start, firm snow, and off the slopes before the afternoon. There is no shelter, the basin is a cold sink, and there is no easy retreat except the way you came. This is a competent-party option in a narrow window, not a general-purpose camp.
